previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, chronic pancreatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for left upper quadrant and flank pain lasting three days. The pain was atypical for her usual Crohn’s flares, which are typically right-sided. Imaging showed mild cecal inflammation consistent with a Crohn’s flare and pancreatic ductal dilation due to chronic pancreatitis. Muscle spasm and constipation were also contributing factors. She was managed with pain control, a short course of antibiotics, a bowel regimen, and a muscle relaxant. An MRCP was performed but limited due to lack of intravenous contrast; no mass was identified. Her pain improved, kidney function stabilized, and she was discharged home with services on a stable condition. Medications were adjusted, including switching from oxycodone to Percocet due to a national shortage, with appropriate liver safety counseling.
